Front: What is a generic class in Java?
Back: A class that declares one or more type parameters in `<>` after the class name, allowing it to work with different types while providing compile-time type safety.

Front: What is the syntax for declaring a generic class?
Back: `class Box<T> { private T value; }` — the type parameter `T` appears after the class name and can be used anywhere a normal type is used in the class body.

Front: What happens when you use a raw type instead of a generic type?
Back: Generic safety is disabled. The compiler emits unchecked warnings and a `ClassCastException` can occur at runtime.

Front: What is a generic method?
Back: A method that introduces its own type parameters (placed before the return type), independent of any class-level type parameters.

Front: Where is the type parameter declared in a generic method?
Back: Before the return type: `public static <T> T identity(T obj) { return obj; }`

Front: What is a generic interface?
Back: An interface that declares type parameters, forcing all implementations to work with a specific concrete type.

Front: Name three generic interfaces in the JDK.
Back: `Comparable<T>`, `Comparator<T>`, `Iterable<T>`, `Function<T,R>` (any three).

Front: What is a type parameter?
Back: A placeholder name (e.g. `T`, `E`, `K`) declared in `<>` that represents an unknown type within a generic class, method, or interface.

Front: What letter convention is used for element type in collections?
Back: `E` — element; used by `List<E>`, `Set<E>`, `Queue<E>`.

Front: What letter convention is used for key and value in maps?
Back: `K` for key and `V` for value — used by `Map<K,V>`.

Front: How do you declare a class with multiple type parameters?
Back: Comma-separate them: `class Pair<K, V> { private K key; private V value; }`

Front: What is a bounded type parameter?
Back: A type parameter with an upper bound: `<T extends Bound>`. Restricts valid type arguments to subtypes of `Bound` and allows calling methods of `Bound` on `T`.

Front: What does `<T extends Number>` allow you to do inside the method?
Back: Call any method defined on `Number` (e.g. `doubleValue()`, `intValue()`) directly on `T` values.

Front: What happens if you pass a `List<String>` to a method expecting `<T extends Number>`?
Back: Compile error — `String` does not extend `Number`, so the bound is violated.

Front: What is the syntax for multiple bounds on a type parameter?
Back: `<T extends Class & Interface1 & Interface2>` — the class must come first.

Front: What is an unbounded wildcard `<?>`?
Back: Represents any unknown type. Useful when the code only needs to read elements as `Object` and does not care about the actual type.

Front: Can you add elements to a `List<?>`?
Back: No (except `null`). The actual type is unknown so adding any typed element would be unsafe.

Front: What does `<? extends T>` mean?
Back: An upper-bounded wildcard: some unknown type that is a subtype of `T`. The collection is a producer — you can read `T` values but cannot add them.

Front: What does `<? super T>` mean?
Back: A lower-bounded wildcard: some unknown type that is a supertype of `T`. The collection is a consumer — you can add `T` values but reading gives only `Object`.

Front: What does PECS stand for?
Back: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

Front: When should you use `<? extends T>` according to PECS?
Back: When a parameter produces (you only read) `T` values — e.g. a source list you iterate over.

Front: When should you use `<? super T>` according to PECS?
Back: When a parameter consumes (you only write) `T` values — e.g. a destination list you add into.

Front: What wildcard does `Collections.copy(dest, src)` use for `dest` and why?
Back: `List<? super T>` because `dest` consumes (receives) `T` values. PECS: Consumer Super.

Front: What wildcard does `Collections.copy(dest, src)` use for `src` and why?
Back: `List<? extends T>` because `src` produces `T` values for reading. PECS: Producer Extends.

Front: What is type erasure in Java?
Back: The process by which the compiler removes generic type information after type-checking. Bytecode uses raw types and inserted casts instead.

Front: What does the compiler insert during type erasure when you call `list.get(0)` on a `List<String>`?
Back: An explicit cast `(String)` before returning the element, because the bytecode sees `List.get()` returning `Object`.

Front: Why can't you check `obj instanceof List<String>` at runtime?
Back: Because generic type information is erased at runtime; the JVM only sees `List`, not `List<String>`.

Front: What is a raw type?
Back: A generic class or interface used without any type arguments (e.g. `List` instead of `List<String>`), disabling all generic type safety.

Front: What runtime error can raw types cause?
Back: `ClassCastException` — adding a value of the wrong type is allowed at compile time but fails when the cast is inserted by the JVM.

Front: In what situation is using a raw type unavoidable?
Back: Inside `instanceof` checks — `obj instanceof List` (raw) is necessary; `obj instanceof List<String>` is a compile error.

Front: Can you create an array of a type parameter? Why?
Back: No. `new T[10]` is a compile error. Arrays carry their component type at runtime, but `T` is erased, so the JVM cannot enforce array-store type safety.

Front: Can you use primitive types as type arguments in generics?
Back: No. `List<int>` is a compile error. Use wrapper types (`List<Integer>`) and rely on autoboxing.

Front: Can a class have a static field of its type parameter type?
Back: No. `static T instance;` is a compile error. Static members are shared across all parameterizations of the class.

Front: Why can't you overload two methods that differ only in generic type arguments?
Back: After type erasure both methods have identical signatures, causing a duplicate method compile error.

Front: What is the work-around for creating a generic array `new T[n]`?
Back: Either use `List<T>`, or cast: `(T[]) new Object[n]`, or use `Array.newInstance(clazz, n)` with a `Class<T>` token.
